title: Use language and communication in occupational learning programmes

lessons.title: Being a learner at work
lessons.html:
Learning on the job

When you join a learnership or skills programme, you learn in two places: in the training room and on the work floor. At the abattoir, the grain silo or the packhouse, you will learn new skills from facilitators, mentors and experienced co-workers. Language is the tool you use to learn. You listen, read, ask, write and speak.

Know what you must learn

Each programme is made of unit standards or modules. Each one has outcomes, which are the things you must be able to do at the end. Ask your facilitator to explain the outcomes in simple words. For example: 'At the end you must be able to clean and sanitise a cutting table and record it.'

Ways to learn

  • Listening to the facilitator and mentor.
  • Watching someone do a task, then doing it yourself while they watch.
  • Reading the learner guide, work instructions and notices.
  • Practising on the job until you are confident.
  • Talking with other learners about what you learnt.

Learn in your strongest language

Many learner guides are in English. If English is not your first language, it is fine to discuss the work in your home language with other learners first, then explain it in English. Make a list of new English words with the meaning in your own language. Many workplace words have special meanings, such as 'carcass', 'contamination', 'moisture content' or 'grading'.

Do not be shy to say you do not understand. Every good learner asks questions. The facilitator is there to help you.

lessons.title: Taking notes and asking questions
lessons.html:
Capturing what you learn

You will forget much of what you hear in a training session unless you write some of it down. Notes do not need to be beautiful. They need to help you remember.

Simple note-taking tips

  • Write the date and topic at the top.
  • Write key words, not full sentences.
  • Use arrows, numbers and small drawings.
  • Write down steps in order, for example the steps to put on protective clothing.
  • Underline new words and find their meaning later.
  • Leave space to add more after the session.

Asking good questions

Asking questions shows that you are thinking. Good questions are clear and short:

  • 'Can you show me again how to set the scale to zero?'
  • 'What does cross-contamination mean?'
  • 'Why must we wash our boots before entering the clean area?'

Use question words: what, why, how, when, where and who. If you are nervous to ask in front of the group, write down your question and ask the facilitator at break.

Working in a group

Many activities are done in groups. In a group:

  • Listen to each person and let everyone speak.
  • Share your own experience from the workplace.
  • Agree on who will report back to the class.
  • Disagree politely: 'I see it another way because…'

Group work helps you learn from other people's experience. A co-worker who has worked in a poultry plant for ten years knows many things that are not in the book.

lessons.title: Assessment, feedback and your portfolio
lessons.html:
Showing what you can do

To get credits, you must show an assessor that you are competent. This is called assessment. It is not a test to catch you out. It is a way to prove your skills.

Types of assessment

  • Written tasks: answering questions in your workbook.
  • Practical observation: the assessor watches you do the job.
  • Oral questions: the assessor asks you to explain what you are doing and why.
  • Workplace evidence: checklists, logbooks and signed statements from your supervisor.

Your portfolio of evidence

Your evidence goes into a file called a portfolio of evidence, or PoE. Keep it neat and complete. Put your name and ID number on every page. Do not copy another learner's answers. Your work must be your own. Copying is cheating and your assessment will not count.

Understanding instructions in assessments

WordWhat it asks
ListWrite a short list of points
DescribeSay what something is like or how it is done
ExplainSay why or how, give reasons
DemonstrateShow by doing it

Using feedback

After assessment the assessor gives feedback. If you are 'not yet competent', it means you need more practice, not that you failed for ever. Listen to what you must improve, ask questions, practise and try again. You also have the right to appeal if you feel the assessment was unfair.

Key points

  • Find out the outcomes you must achieve.
  • Take short notes with key words, steps and new words.
  • Ask clear questions using what, why and how.
  • Your portfolio of evidence must be your own work.
  • Use feedback to improve; 'not yet competent' means more practice is needed.
